title: Make routines to dissect some data types exportable
description:
I developed internal plugin dissector and need to use several types.
That is why made them as WS_DLL_PUBLIC.

notes.body: I have no problem with making them external but you are probably better of making your private dissector internal and distribute your own internal windows installer. In any case the plugin will only work with specific versions of wirashark.

Yes, at the beginning I'm planning distribute plugin with internal installer. But later (after commit will be merged and new Wireshark's version offically released) plugin will be distributed as DLL. Just copy to user's wireshark config directory.

The only reason you would be better off distributing your own build of Wireshark is because dissector plugin support in Wireshark is rather limited and broken in some ways (this is one of them).

Obviously recompiling and redistributing a plugin every X.Y release (if that, but that is the requirement right now) is superior in many different dimensions to recompiling and redistributing the whole of Wireshark every X.Y.Z release. This is rather obvious.

Not to me it isn't. It's just as easy to build and distribute the complete
installer and avoids pitfals of non exporten symbols and windows dll
problems. I switched to this method some 10-15 years ago for our internal
wireshark version.

skrev:

I don't know what windows DLL problems are. The pitfalls of non-exported symbols is a technical defect in Wireshark and bundling plugins is called a workaround in that case.

I doubt 10-15 years ago you had other options available to write Wireshark plugins but in any case if you are already a large enough organization to spend resources to maintain a dedicated internal version of Wireshark for reasons, then your "plugin" is just another form of source code modification and not much different from a private built-in dissector. I do not know why you would even use a plugin in that case but whatever.

Anyway I don't feel like writing a thesis on why extensibility is a desirable property but it certainly doesn't equate to everyone having to maintain a custom internal Wireshark version, which is what you are always pushing for as if this is the general consensus whenever someone raises an issue involving improving plugin support.
changed title from **Make {-some-} types exportable** to **Make {+routines to dissect some data+} types exportable**

added 19 commits
  • bcf5bc83...5cf528c8 - 18 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • 44539389 - Make some types exportable
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/18529/diffs?diff_id=1219065230&start_sha=bcf5bc836d3c1438a49b5cf682ff6508c6887133)

This addresses one specific situation but in my opinion the proper fix would be to use default (i.e public) symbol visibility for libwireshark, be conscious of good naming practices and install the library to a private (non-default) system path. The usual (good) reasons to hide shared library symbols are not really applicable here. And besides symbols can still be hidden with WS_DLL_LOCAL if necessary. Exposing functions on an ad-hoc basis without rhyme or reason is not a viable long-term solution.

> the proper fix would be to use default (i.e public) symbol visibility for libwireshark,

Default symbol visibility from a DLL is not public under Windows, though CMake has added some options that make it slightly easier to export all symbols than the traditional workaround used. (https://www.kitware.com//create-dlls-on-windows-without-declspec-using-new-cmake-export-all-feature/)

We don't properly export all the global variables for Windows currently, so that, e.g., the true_false_strings can't be used in a plugin on Windows, though that should be fixable.
Thanks for the feedback. I was focusing on GCC/Linux to simplify and because that is what I know best but the general idea is still applicable to Windows, although the mechanics may and do differ.

I'm just proposing to invert the default policy and adapt some practices to fit that. Simple enough and workable within the what is practical and realistic in this project. Seems to me that some devs decided to blindly apply ideas and concepts presented in the GCC/Wiki on symbol visibility without due consideration but that is just my personal speculation.

> the general idea is still applicable to Windows, although the mechanics may and do differ.

The problem is that Windows doesn't *really* let you export and import *data*, as opposed to functions, from a DLL.

> In the case of data, ` __declspec(dllimport)` is a convenience item that removes a layer of indirection. When you import data from a DLL, you still have to go through the import address table.

It's really accessing it through a pointer, and this is just some syntactic sugar:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/importing-data-using-declspec-dllimport

However:

> You cannot initialize a static data pointer with the address of a data object declared with the dllimport attribute. *(ed: Because the address is not the address of the data object but that of the DLL import thunk)*

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-language/rules-and-limitations-for-dllimport-dllexport

> One drawback to using this attribute is that a pointer to a variable marked as dllimport cannot be used as a constant address. 
https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Microsoft-Windows-Function-Attributes.html

This means, for example, that even though the various `true_false_strings` are marked `WS_DLL_PUBLIC` (and even if the definitions were marked `WS_DLL_PUBLIC_DEF`), we could not use a pointer to those variables as a constant in a plugin for initializing a `static hf_register_info hf[]` as we normally do. `TFS(&tfs_on_off)` cannot be used to initialize the hf, which is the normal usage.

I recognize that global variables are a problem with Windows DLLs, so those need to be refactored if we want to make them accessible to plugins on Windows, but it is an orthogonal issue. Doing what Anders suggests (unless it is a monolithic build obviously) doesn't fix that either.

The reason I proposed using public visibility (which is possible on Windows, particularly easy with CMake as you noted) is not to fix problems with global variables, it is this:

> Exposing functions on an ad-hoc basis without rhyme or reason is not a viable long-term solution.

Hiding symbols to protect our internal libwireshark shared library interface from ourselves is nice but convenient easy plugin development (other than global variables like TFS, which require different solutions) is nicer and has no real drawbacks.
